network.overall_strategy: The network constructs L-proline from plausible prebiotic feedstocks via a diverse set of pathways: homologation, reductive amination, Strecker-type transformations, and surface-catalyzed cyclization, spanning hydrothermal, surface, and prebiotic microenvironment conditions. Each pathway is atom- and charge-balanced, with byproducts explicitly specified throughout. By leveraging C1 and C2 sources (HCN, glyoxylate, formaldehyde/acrolein, NH3, CO2), the network systematically builds the 5-membered pyrrolidine backbone and introduces chirality using plausible geochemical selectors.

reactions.name: Glycine synthesis via Strecker reaction
reactions.mechanism: Formaldehyde condenses with HCN and NH3 to form an aminonitrile, which hydrolyzes to glycine, yielding water as byproduct.
reactions.reasoning: Strecker synthesis is prebiotically credible (Miller, 1953; Bada, 2013). Montmorillonite enhances yields and supports selectivity.

reactions.name: Alanine synthesis from glyoxylate by homologation
reactions.mechanism: Glycine reacts with formaldehyde in an FeS-catalyzed reductive amination to yield alanine and water.
reactions.reasoning: Homologation reactions are seen with Fe/Ni minerals in hydrothermal vents (Muchowska, 2017; Preiner, 2020).

reactions.name: Aminopropionaldehyde formation by reduction of alanine
reactions.mechanism: Reductive decarboxylation of alanine yields 3-aminopropanal and water.
reactions.reasoning: Metal-catalyzed decarboxylation and hydrogenation are supported in vent environments (Huber & Wächtershäuser, 1997).

reactions.name: Cyclization of 3-aminopropanal to pyrroline intermediate
reactions.mechanism: Intramolecular condensation of 3-aminopropanal forms Δ1-pyrroline-2-carboxylic acid.
reactions.reasoning: This cyclization step is established in non-enzymatic settings (Peltzer et al., 1984).

reactions.name: Reduction of pyrroline-2-carboxylic acid to L-proline
reactions.mechanism: Hydrogenation at the imine double bond produces L-proline.
reactions.reasoning: Non-enzymatic reduction with transition metals is strongly substantiated (Varadarajan et al., 2022).

reactions.name: Strecker synthesis of γ-aminobutyric acid
reactions.mechanism: Propanal, HCN and NH3 react via Strecker to give γ-aminobutyraldehyde, hydrolyzed to γ-aminobutyric acid; water produced.
reactions.reasoning: Supported by surface-catalyzed Strecker chemistry (Chyba & Sagan, 1992; Saladino et al., 2012).

reactions.name: Dehydration to aminocrotonic acid
reactions.mechanism: Surface-catalyzed elimination of water produces aminocrotonic acid from γ-aminobutyric acid.
reactions.reasoning: Surface-facilitated dehydration is common in wet-dry cycles (Lambert, 2008).

reactions.name: Cyclization to proline (via aminocrotonic acid)
reactions.mechanism: The aminocrotonic acid cyclizes directly to proline under mild heating, no catalyst.
reactions.reasoning: This spontaneous cyclization has precedent (Meierhenrich et al., 2005; Saladino et al., 2012).

reactions.name: Glycine chain elongation via acrolein condensation
reactions.mechanism: Glycine condenses with maleic acid (model for acrolein oxidized) to form γ-aminobutyric acid and release CO2.
reactions.reasoning: Borate minerals stabilize intermediates and promote elongation (Kim & Benner, 2017).

reactions.name: Amination of butanal to yield 4-aminobutanal
reactions.mechanism: Reductive amination of propanal with ammonia forms 4-aminobutanal.
reactions.reasoning: Supported by hydrothermal nickel-catalyzed amination experiments (Muchowska, 2019).

reactions.name: 4-aminobutanal cyclization to Δ1-pyrroline-2-carboxylate
reactions.mechanism: Imine cyclization with CO2 to produce Δ1-pyrroline-2-carboxylate and water.
reactions.reasoning: Cyclization/carboxylation with CO2 is plausible prebiotically, see Peltzer (1984), chemistry of imine-carboxylate cyclization.

reactions.name: Alternative Strecker synthesis yielding alanine
reactions.mechanism: Glyoxylate, HCN, and NH3 undergo Strecker reaction yielding racemic alanine (DL-alanine) and water.
reactions.reasoning: Strecker alanine is robust in surface and evaporitic pools (Bada, 2013).

pathways.name: Hydrothermal glycine→alanine reduction/cyclization route
pathways.description: Classic route using Strecker glycine, formaldehyde homologation, reduction, cyclization, and hydrogenation to L-proline.

pathways.name: Surface Strecker γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA) route
pathways.description: Glycine chain-elongated to γ-aminobutyric acid via acrolein/maleic acid; dehydration and cyclization to proline.

pathways.name: Direct Strecker γ-aminobutyric acid/proline path
pathways.description: Strecker synthesis from propanal to GABA, then dehydration and cyclization to L-proline.

pathways.name: Reductive hydrothermal amination/cyclization pathway
pathways.description: Alanine formed via homologation, reduced to 3-aminopropionaldehyde, cyclized to proline.

pathways.name: Aldehyde amination/cyclization with hydrothermal CO2
pathways.description: Propanal aminated to 4-aminobutanal, cyclized with CO2 to pyrroline intermediate, reduced to proline.

pathways.name: Alternative Strecker alanine/homologation route
pathways.description: Glyoxylate undergoes Strecker to DL-alanine, then via hydrothermal reactions to proline.

pathways.name: Alanine—>aminopropanal direct reduction route
pathways.description: Alanine (homologated from glycine or by Strecker) provides aminopropanal via NiS catalysis, then sequential cyclization and reduction.

pathways.name: Maleic acid chain extension pathway
pathways.description: Maleic acid condenses with glycine (borate-catalyzed) to GABA, through aminocrotonic acid, cyclizes to proline.

pathways.name: Propanal-based amination/cyclization
pathways.description: Propanal undergoes Strecker-type amination to GABA, dehydrated to aminocrotonic acid, cyclized to proline.

pathways.name: Cyclization with exogenous CO2 (butanal amination)
pathways.description: Butanal is aminated to 4-aminobutanal, immediately cyclized with CO2 to pyrroline-2-carboxylate, reduced to L-proline.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: P1 includes a series of unbalanced reactions (rxn_001–rxn_004). Key intermediates are identified and the pathway is logical, but mass balance failures throughout (except rxn_005, which is reasonable) harm chemical feasibility. Environmental assignments largely make sense. Correction of atom balances and some mechanistic steps is needed.
suggestions: Fix atom imbalances, specify byproducts.
Clarify cyclization step mechanism and conserve mass.
Check intermediate formulas for accuracy.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This pathway leverages plausible surface reactions but fails atom/charge balance at the Strecker, dehydration, and cyclization steps. Reactant selection is logical and steps are in a plausible prebiotic order. Correction of chemical formulas and product accounting is required for higher feasibility.
suggestions: Balance each step for all atoms.
Provide mechanistic/experimental support for the cyclization.
Review the stoichiometry for intermediates.

The progression to proline is sensible but chemically incomplete without full atom conservation. Propose balancing all reactions and clarify any ambiguous cyclization chemistry.

suggestions: Complete pathway definition and balance all steps.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Exogenous CO2 as a cyclization agent is a conceptually reasonable path, but C atom imbalance in rxn_010 is persistent. With correct mass balance, this pathway would become competitive.
suggestions: Revise amination steps to balance C atoms.
Clarify stepwise reaction details including byproducts.

evaluation.network_feedback: The network captures a rich and logical range of prebiotic scenarios and chemical steps for L-proline synthesis. However, network validity and chemical feasibility are critically compromised by pervasive atom/charge balance failures at almost every step outside the chain extension. Several intermediates also have structural or formula inconsistencies (notably with RDKit parsing failures). Environmental assignments and progression are credible throughout and the strategies are creative, but the network cannot be approved until each reaction conserves mass and charge, and all intermediates are clearly defined and matched to their formulas. Major revision is needed to correct stoichiometry, complete unbalanced or ambiguous steps, and ensure every transformation is chemically rigorous. Literature alignment cannot be meaningfully scored in the absence of balanced, mechanistically specified reactions.
